evidence.label: A directional zero–one law for finite-range-dependent random environments
A directional zero–one law under strict ellipticity

headline: A walk in a random environment escapes in a given direction with probability 0 or 1, and escape forces positive speed.
scope: Nearest-neighbour walks on the integer grid; the zero–one laws need dimension 3 or more, the speed result dimension 2 or more.
plain: Picture a walker on a grid whose step odds are set at random, once, at every site. One question asks whether the chance of drifting off in a fixed direction must be 0 or 1. Another asks whether drifting off forces a positive average speed. These papers answer yes in key cases. Lean has checked the iid zero–one law and the speed result; the dependent-environment extension is not checked.
doesNot: This does not give the zero–one law in dimension 2 beyond earlier work, or for environments with long-range dependence.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Kalikow, the first directional transience results
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles two central problems for random walks in iid random environments, with the main statements checked in Lean.

explanation:
Start on a line of sites. At each site, flip a fair coin once and keep the result forever. Heads makes that site push right with chance 0.9. Tails makes it push right with chance only 0.3. A walker then steps left or right using the odds at its current site. Does it drift off to the right? A classical test by Solomon looks at the ratio of left to right odds. The ratios here are 1/9 and 7/3. The average of their logarithms is about −0.675, which is negative. So the walker escapes to the right. But the plain average of the ratios is about 1.22, at least 1. That makes its long-run speed zero. Traps of left-pushing sites slow it so much that it covers distance more slowly than any fixed rate.

This is a random walk in a random environment. The environment is the list of step odds at every site, drawn once and then held fixed. Directional transience means the walker eventually leaves every half-space behind it in a chosen direction[1]. Ballisticity asks for more: steady progress at a positive speed. The line example shows the two can differ, already in one dimension[2].

Two old questions sit here for higher dimensions. First, can the chance of escaping in one direction lie strictly between 0 and 1? Kalikow, with Sznitman and Zerner, showed only that escape in one of the two opposite directions has chance 0 or 1[3]. In two dimensions, Zerner and Merkl proved the full zero–one law. Their argument uses crossings of paths in the plane[4]. Second, does escape in one direction force positive speed? Fribergh and Kious stated this as a conjecture in 2016[5].

The second paper takes the first question. Averaging over the environment makes the walk remember. Returning to a site reveals more about its odds[6]. The paper proves the zero–one law in every dimension from 3 up[7]. The environment must be iid, meaning each site's odds are drawn independently from one fixed recipe. Every step must have positive chance, but no common lower bound is needed[8].

The third paper takes the second question. Here the odds must be uniformly elliptic: every step has chance at least some fixed κ above 0. It proves that escape in one direction gives a fixed limiting velocity, pointing into that direction[9]. This holds in every dimension from 2 up. The obstacle was that walks split into independent pieces only gives finite pieces. It does not show their average length is finite. The proof first controls how far a piece wanders and only later how long it lasts[10].

The first paper extends the zero–one law beyond independence. Sites may depend on each other, but only within a fixed distance[11]. Correlations that merely fade are not enough. Bramson, Zeitouni and Zerner built environments with slowly fading correlations where escape in each of two opposite directions has positive chance[12].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked formal versions of the iid zero–one law under strict ellipticity, for dimension 3 and up. It has also checked that escape implies a positive velocity in dimension 2 and up, under uniform ellipticity. The finite-range dependent extension is not formalized. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major. The iid zero–one law and the speed result have Lean checks; the finite-range extension does not, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Step odds placed at every site of a grid by a random draw, then held fixed while the walker moves.
The walker eventually moves off forever in a chosen direction, leaving every half-space behind it.
Moving off in a direction at a positive average speed, not just eventually.
A result saying an event has probability exactly 0 or exactly 1, never anything in between.
Every allowed step has positive chance; uniform ellipticity adds a common lower bound for those chances.
Independent and identically distributed: each site's odds are drawn separately from the same recipe.
Sites far enough apart have independent odds; nearby sites may be linked.
